title: Was shee thy God, that her thou didst obey Before his voice
short: The Son, judging Adam, names his sin as a kind of idolatry: he put Eve in God's place and abdicated the 'part And person' of ruler.
body: When Adam blames Eve ('Shee gave me of the Tree, and I did eate', Genesis 3:12), the Son replies: 'Was shee thy God, that her thou didst obey Before his voice, or was shee made thy guide, Superior, or but equal, that to her Thou did'st resigne thy Manhood'. The Dartmouth edition notes the implied charge of idolatry and the Pauline background (1 Corinthians 11:8-9). Verity explains that 'part And person' are theatrical terms: it was Adam's role (Latin persona) to govern. The rebuke repeats almost exactly Raphael's warning in 8.561-78, which Verity cross-refers, and settles the poem's verdict on 9.999: Adam's love was not wrong, but its ordering was. Eve, asked 'What is this which thou hast done?', answers simply, 'The Serpent me beguil'd and I did eate' (Genesis 3:13).

anchor: Her Seed shall bruise thy head
title: Her Seed shall bruise thy head, thou bruise his heel
short: The curse on the serpent (Genesis 3:15), read by Christians as the first promise of Christ's victory over Satan: the 'protevangelium'.
body: The Son pronounces the curse of Genesis 3:15 'in mysterious terms': 'Between Thee and the Woman I will put Enmitie, and between thine and her Seed; Her Seed shall bruise thy head, thou bruise his heel'. Christian tradition called this the protevangelium, the first announcement of the gospel, reading the 'seed' as Christ, born of a woman, who would defeat Satan at the cost of suffering; the Dartmouth edition notes the term and its supersessionist reading of the Hebrew text. The narrator explains the fulfilment, 'When Jesus son of Mary second Eve, Saw Satan fall like Lightning down from Heav'n' (Luke 10:18), and triumphed over 'Principalities and Powers' (Colossians 2:15; Ephesians 2:2), as Verity documents. Verity also quotes Bentley's regret that Milton did not make the resurrection the subject of Paradise Regained. Adam and Eve slowly come to understand the promise (10.1030-40; 12.375-85).

title: As Father of his Familie he clad Thir nakedness ... the forme of servant
short: Having judged them, the Son clothes Adam and Eve in animal skins, taking 'the form of servant' as he later will in washing his disciples' feet.
body: Genesis 3:21 says that God made coats of skins and clothed Adam and Eve. Milton makes the Son, 'pitying how they stood Before him naked', clothe them, 'As Father of his Familie', 'not disdaind to begin Thenceforth the forme of servant to assume, As when he wash'd his servants feet'. Verity gives the sources: Philippians 2:7 ('took upon him the form of a servant') and John 13:5 (the washing of the disciples' feet). Whether the beasts were 'slain, Or as the Snake with youthful Coate repaid' is left open; Verity notes that in Eden animals had not yet killed. The Son also covers their 'inward nakedness' with his 'Robe of righteousness' (Isaiah 61:10). The tender scene answers the harshness of the sentence and anticipates the incarnation.

title: the Mole immense ... a Bridge Of length prodigious
short: Sin and Death build a causeway over Chaos from Hell to the world, petrifying its materials with Death's Gorgon-like mace and binding them with asphalt.
body: Sensing Satan's success, Sin and Death fly out of Hell and build 'the Mole immense', a causeway (Latin moles), across Chaos. Death smites the floating soil 'with his Mace petrific, cold and dry', as with a trident, and fixes it 'firm as Delos floating once', the island that Poseidon raised and Zeus chained to the sea-bed (Verity); 'his look' binds it 'with Gorgonian rigor', petrifying like the Gorgon's gaze, and 'Asphaltic slime' (bitumen, the 'slime' of Genesis 11:3) cements it. Verity notes Johnson's objection that this was too material a work for allegorical figures, and Burke's use of 'the cold, dry, petrific mace' against revolutionary philosophy. The bridge fulfils the narrator's prophecy at 2.1024-30 and makes Hell's road to earth easy for all later sinners.

title: Xerxes, the Libertie of Greece to yoke ... over Hellespont Bridging his way
short: Sin and Death's bridge is compared to the bridge of boats with which the Persian king Xerxes crossed the Hellespont to enslave Greece.
body: The causeway is compared, 'if great things to small may be compar'd' (a Virgilian formula, Verity notes), to the bridge by which 'Xerxes, the Libertie of Greece to yoke, From Susa his Memnonian Palace high Came to the Sea, and over Hellespont Bridging his way, Europe with Asia joyn'd, And scourg'd with many a stroak th' indignant waves'. Verity cites Herodotus 7.33-36: when a storm destroyed his first bridge, Xerxes ordered the Hellespont to be given three hundred lashes and fettered. Susa was the Persian royal city, its citadel traditionally built by Memnon. The comparison is political as well as visual: the bridge from Hell, like Xerxes' bridge, is an instrument of tyranny over liberty, joining two realms that nature had divided.

title: by wondrous Art Pontifical
greek: Latin pontifex, 'bridge-maker'; title of the Pope
short: 'Pontifical' means bridge-building (Latin pons + facere), with a sarcastic pun on the Pope, the Pontifex, as a builder of roads to Hell.
body: The bridge is built 'by wondrous Art Pontifical, a ridge of pendent Rock'. Verity explains the literal sense, 'bridge-making', from Latin pons ('bridge') and facere ('make'), and notes the suggestion of a sarcastic allusion to the Pope, whose title Pontifex Maximus derived from the Roman college of priests; Satan later praises the work as 'this glorious Work' and Sin is called 'Pontifice' at 10.348. The Dartmouth edition treats the pun as intended, associating the papacy with Sin, Death and Hell. It fits the anti-Catholic satire of the Paradise of Fools (3.444-97), where the souls of friars blow away from Heaven's gate, and the 'conclave' of Book I.

anchor: By Astracan over the Snowie Plaines
title: As when the Tartar from his Russian Foe By Astracan ... or Bactrian Sophi
short: The devils withdraw to Pandaemonium like Tartars retreating from the Russians, or the Persian Shah retreating before the Turks.
body: Two contemporary military images describe the devils abandoning their outposts for the capital: 'As when the Tartar from his Russian Foe By Astracan over the Snowie Plaines Retires, or Bactrian Sophi from the hornes Of Turkish Crescent, leaves all waste beyond The Realme of Aladule, in his retreate To Tauris or Casbeen'. Verity explains: 'Sophi' is the Shah of Persia (Bactria standing for Persia), 'the hornes Of Turkish Crescent' are the Ottoman armies under the crescent ensign, Aladule is Greater Armenia, named after its last king, and Tauris and Casbeen are Tabriz and Kazvin; Persia and the Ottomans fought through the sixteenth century. Verity suggests Milton took such names from Mercator's Atlas. The Russian details reflect his own History of Moscovia.

title: A dismal universal hiss: the devils turned to serpents
short: Satan expects applause for his triumph and hears instead a universal hiss: he and all his followers are transformed into serpents.
body: Satan reports his victory in Pandaemonium and waits for 'universal shout and high applause', but hears 'A dismal universal hiss, the sound Of public scorn'. He falls on his belly, 'A monstrous Serpent', punished 'in the shape he sin'd, According to his doom' (Genesis 3:14), and the devils are changed with him. Verity cites Newton's suggestion that Milton recalled Ovid's account of Cadmus becoming a serpent (Metamorphoses 4.576-603) and Todd's comparison with Dante's metamorphoses of thieves into serpents (Inferno 24-25), which Verity finds more repulsive. He also notes the sibilant alliteration of the passage, which makes the reader hear the hiss. The scene is the poem's most explicit poetic justice, a punishment that is also a comic deflation of the hero's triumph.

anchor: Scorpion and Asp, and Amphisbaena dire
title: Scorpion and Asp, and Amphisbaena dire, Cerastes hornd, Hydrus, and Ellops drear, And Dipsas
greek: Greek amphisbaina, 'going both ways'; kerastês, 'horned'; hudros; dipsas, 'thirsty'
short: A catalogue of the venomous serpents of Libya, taken from Lucan, who said they sprang from the drops of the Gorgon Medusa's blood.
body: The swarm of transformed devils is named with the snakes of classical natural history: the scorpion and asp; the amphisbaena, supposed to have a head at each end (Greek 'going both ways'), which Sir Thomas Browne doubted; the horned cerastes; the water-snake hydrus; the ellops; and the dipsas, whose bite caused raging thirst (Greek dipsa). Verity explains each and identifies the source: Lucan's catalogue of the serpents of Libya (Pharsalia 9.700-33), which sprang from the drops of Medusa's blood as Perseus flew over Africa with her head (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.617-20). 'Ophiusa', 'snake island', was an old name of islands infested by serpents. The catalogue reverses the catalogue of Book I: the proud names have become a list of reptiles.

title: Now Dragon grown, larger then whom the Sun Ingenderd in the Pythian Vale on slime, Huge Python
short: Satan, transformed, is larger than the Python, the serpent bred from the mud after the Flood and killed by Apollo at Delphi.
body: Satan, 'now Dragon grown', exceeds 'whom the Sun Ingenderd in the Pythian Vale on slime, Huge Python'. Verity cites Ovid's account of the monstrous serpent Python, born from the slime left by the flood of Deucalion and warmed by the sun, which Apollo killed with his arrows near Delphi, founding the Pythian games (Metamorphoses 1.434-51). 'Dragon' recalls 'the great dragon ... that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan' of Revelation 12:9, as Verity notes. The Python appeared earlier in the poem's mythology through the 'Pythian fields' of the devils' games (2.530). Even reduced to a serpent, Satan keeps a residue of his former greatness, 'and his Power no less he seem'd Above the rest still to retain'.

title: the fruitage fair ... like that which grew Neer that bituminous Lake where Sodom flam'd
short: The devils, tormented with hunger, eat illusory fruit that turns to ashes, like the legendary apples of the Dead Sea near Sodom.
body: A grove springs up in Hell laden with fruit 'like that which grew Neer that bituminous Lake where Sodom flam'd'. The ravenous serpents climb thick as 'the snaky locks That curld Megaera' (one of the Furies, whose hair was snakes, as Verity notes), but chew 'bitter Ashes' that they spit out 'with spattering noise'. Verity explains the allusion to the 'apples of the Dead Sea', fair to the eye but turning to ashes when touched, which Milton had used in Eikonoklastes; the legend is reported by Josephus (Jewish War 4.484) and echoes Deuteronomy 32:32, 'their vine is of the vine of Sodom ... their grapes are grapes of gall'. The punishment imitates the crime: the devils are deceived by a fruit as they deceived Eve, and the torment is to be renewed yearly.

title: Ophion with Eurynome, the wide-Encroaching Eve perhaps
short: The pagan myth of Ophion and Eurynome, first rulers of Olympus overthrown by Saturn, is read as a garbled memory of the serpent and Eve.
body: The story of the serpent's triumph survived among 'the Heathen', who 'fabl'd how the Serpent, whom they calld Ophion with Eurynome, the wide-Encroaching Eve perhaps, had first the rule Of high Olympus, thence by Saturn driv'n And Ops, ere yet Dictaean Jove was born'. Verity explains that Ophion's name means 'serpent' and that Newton found the myth in Apollonius' Argonautica (1.503-09), where Orpheus sings of Ophion and Eurynome ruling Olympus before Cronos (Saturn) and Rhea (Ops) cast them out. Newton, quoted by Verity, explains 'wide-Encroaching' as a pun on Eurynome, 'wide-ruling', suggesting Eve's overreaching. Dictaean Jove is Zeus, raised on Mount Dicte in Crete. Milton again treats myth as corrupted memory of the true history.

anchor: turn Reines from th' Equinoctial Rode
title: the Sun Was bid turn Reines from th' Equinoctial Rode ... to Taurus with the Seav'n Atlantick Sisters
short: After the Fall angels tilt the cosmos so that the sun's path is oblique to the equator, creating the seasons; Milton gives both Copernican and Ptolemaic explanations.
body: God sends angels to alter the heavens: 'Some say he bid his Angels turne ascanse The Poles of Earth twice ten degrees and more From the Suns Axle; they with labour push'd Oblique the Centric Globe: Som say the Sun Was bid turn Reines from th' Equinoctial Rode'. Verity quotes Masson's explanation: before the Fall the sun's path lay in the plane of the equator, giving eternal spring; afterwards the ecliptic was set at about 23 degrees to it, either by tilting the earth (Copernican) or by moving the sun (Ptolemaic). The sun's new course takes it through the zodiac to Taurus, the Pleiades ('Seav'n Atlantick Sisters', daughters of Atlas), Gemini ('the Spartan Twins', Castor and Pollux) and the 'Tropic Crab' (Cancer), as the Dartmouth edition glosses. Verity notes that some Fathers, and Dante, held that spring was perpetual in Eden.

title: The Sun, as from Thyestean Banquet, turn'd His course intended
short: The sun turns from its course as it did in horror at the banquet where Atreus served Thyestes his own sons: an image of unnatural eating.
body: 'At that tasted Fruit The Sun, as from Thyestean Banquet, turn'd His course intended'. Verity tells the story: Atreus, king of Mycenae, pretending reconciliation with his brother Thyestes, killed Thyestes' sons and served their flesh to him at a banquet; the sun turned back in horror (the tale is the subject of Seneca's Thyestes). Milton suggests that eating the forbidden fruit had a similar cosmic effect. The comparison is shocking in its implied equation: the first parents' eating is, like Thyestes' meal, a feast on their own offspring, since it brings death on all their descendants. Verity discusses the scansion, suggesting Milton elided the vowel, 'Thyest(e)an'.

anchor: Boreas and Caecias and Argestes loud
title: Boreas and Caecias and Argestes loud And Thrascias ... Notus and Afer ... Sirocco, and Libecchio
greek: Greek Boreas, Kaikias, Argestês, Thraskias, Notos; Latin Africus
short: The winds, now let loose to war, are named in a compass of classical and Italian names, from the north and north-east to the south-west.
body: After the Fall the winds break from their 'brazen Dungeon' (Verity compares Aeolus' cave of winds, Aeneid 1.52-63) and fight across the world, from 'Norumbega' (an old name for north-eastern America) and 'the Samoed shoar' (Arctic Siberia, which Milton knew from his History of Moscovia). Verity glosses each: Boreas the north wind, Caecias the north-east, Argestes the north-west, Thrascias the north-north-west (the wind from Thrace); Notus the south, Afer ('the African') the south-west, blowing from Sierra Leone ('Serraliona'), proverbial for storms; Eurus and Zephyr the east and west; Levant and Ponent the winds of sunrise and sunset; and Sirocco and Libecchio, Italian names for Mediterranean winds. The roll of names enacts the 'confusion' of the elements.

title: Did I request thee, Maker, from my Clay To mould me Man
short: In despair Adam asks why he was made without his consent, echoing Isaiah's potter and clay; he then answers himself. Mary Shelley used the lines as the epigraph to Frankenstein.
body: Alone at night Adam laments: 'Did I request thee, Maker, from my Clay To mould me Man, did I sollicite thee From darkness to promote me, or here place In this delicious Garden?' Verity cites Isaiah 45:9, 'Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! ... Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?' Adam's argument is that he should be allowed to return to dust since he did not ask to be made; but he refutes himself: his own son might say the same to him (10.760-65). The long soliloquy (10.720-844) moves through despair towards accepting God's justice. Mary Shelley chose these lines as the epigraph of Frankenstein (1818), where a created being asks the same question of his creator.

title: O Conscience, into what Abyss of fears And horrors hast thou driv'n me
short: Adam's conscience, the 'Umpire' God promised (3.195), drives him to recognise that the fault is his alone; Conscience was a character in Milton's early dramatic drafts.
body: Adam ends his soliloquy: 'O Conscience, into what Abyss of fears And horrors hast thou driv'n me; out of which I find no way, from deep to deeper plung'd!' Verity notes that in each of Milton's early drafts of a tragedy on the Fall, Conscience was one of the allegorical characters. The cry echoes Satan's 'in the lowest deep a lower deep' (4.76), but the difference is crucial: Adam's conscience is the 'Umpire Conscience' that God promised to place in fallen man (3.195), and its pain leads towards repentance, whereas Satan's leads only to despair. Adam has already admitted 'On mee, mee onely, as the sourse and spring Of all corruption, all the blame lights due' (10.832-33), and Eve will soon make the same offer.

title: all but a Rib Crooked by nature ... this fair defect Of Nature
short: Adam turns on Eve with a misogynist tirade: she is a crooked rib from his left side, 'this fair defect Of Nature'; the speech is fallen Adam's, not the narrator's.
body: When Eve approaches, Adam drives her off: 'Out of my sight, thou Serpent', and calls her 'all but a Rib Crooked by nature, bent, as now appears, More to the part sinister from me drawn'. Verity explains the pun on 'sinister', both 'left' (the rib was from Adam's left side, 8.465) and 'unlucky', and the old belief that Adam had a supernumerary thirteenth rib on the left from which Eve was made. He asks why God made 'this noveltie on Earth, this fair defect Of Nature', echoing the Aristotelian idea of woman as an imperfect male, and lists the miseries men will suffer through women. Verity compares Hippolytus' tirade against women in Euripides (Hippolytus 616-68). It is important that this is fallen Adam's despairing rage, which Eve's humility immediately answers.

anchor: Repairing where he judg'd us, prostrate fall
title: prostrate fall Before him reverent, and there confess Humbly our faults
short: Reconciled by Eve's humility, Adam proposes that they return to the place of judgment and repent; the narrator repeats his words as their action.
body: Eve's plea, 'Forsake me not thus, Adam', and her offer to bear all the blame (10.914-36) soften Adam. After rejecting her proposals of childlessness or suicide, he remembers the promise that her seed will bruise the serpent's head and resolves: 'What better can we do, then to the place Repairing where he judg'd us, prostrate fall Before him reverent, and there confess Humbly our faults, and pardon beg, with tears Watering the ground'. The book ends by repeating these lines almost word for word as narrative (10.1098-1104). Verity notes the classical figure of repetition and the oddity that Book XI opens with them standing. The scene is the human counterpart to the Son's self-offering in Book III: the turn from blame to shared repentance begins the recovery.
